title: Multi-Link Operation (MLO)
summary: One connection that holds links in several bands, and moves traffic between them without reconnecting.

opener.promise: One connection with links in several bands
opener.problem: Badge calls break up when the one band a device uses gets busy.

beats.heading: The call that breaks up between units

caption.headline: The call that breaks up between units
caption.takeaway: Choppy badge calls cost clinical time and create repeat pages: a care problem, not just IT.

beats.body:
A nurse takes a call on a [[voice-badge]] while walking to the next unit. The badge is connected to the nearest [[access-point]] on a single band — and on that band, an imaging cart has just started a large upload.

The call's small voice packets now wait in line behind the image. The nurse hears gaps and repeats themselves, or the call drops.
beats.bottomLine: Choppy or dropped badge calls cost clinical time and create repeat pages — a reliability problem for care teams, not just an IT inconvenience.
beats.sceneDescription: An access point on the left connects to a nurse's badge on the right with a single arched link. Large grey blocks from an imaging upload fill the link, and the badge's small voice packets bunch up behind them and stall.

beats.heading: One connection, several radio lanes

caption.headline: One connection, several radio lanes
caption.takeaway: [[mlo|Multi-Link Operation]] lets one connection hold links in 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz{{mlo-bands}}.

beats.body:
[[mlo|Multi-Link Operation]] lets a device and an access point form a single connection with links in more than one band {{mlo-defined-be}}. A Wi-Fi 7 connection can combine links in the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz bands {{mlo-bands}}.

Think of it as one conversation with several lanes open to it. Whether the device uses them at the same time or one at a time depends on its multi-link mode, which comes later in this chapter.
beats.bottomLine: MLO gives each connection spare lanes, so a busy band no longer has to mean a stalled device.
beats.sceneDescription: Two more arched links appear between the access point and the badge, so there are three in total, labelled with their bands. All three belong to the same connection; the voice packets travel on one of them, while the other two stand ready.

questions.q: Is MLO just bonding bands together for speed?
questions.a: Speed is one use, but the bigger gain for clinical traffic is resilience: a device keeps links in several bands{{mlo-bands}}, so urgent packets can move to a free band without reconnecting.

beats.heading: Spread the load, keep a spare lane

caption.headline: Busy band? Traffic takes another lane
caption.takeaway: Voice packets can move to another link without reconnecting{{mlo-tid-mapping}}.
caption.technical: Both ends are [[mld|multi-link devices]] with one association across links; traffic classes can map to links{{mlo-tid-mapping}}.

beats.body:
With several links available, traffic can be **moved to another link** when one band is busy, without the device reconnecting first {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. Devices that can use several links at once can also **spread** traffic across them for more throughput {{str-what}}.

Which link is used is the access point’s and device’s scheduling decision, so results depend on the products and how they are configured.
beats.bottomLine: Urgent traffic gets another chance at the air on a different band, instead of only waiting for one band to clear.
beats.deepDive: Both ends are [[mld|multi-link devices]] (MLDs): an AP MLD is a set of affiliated access points, one per link. The client associates once and keeps a single security context across links; traffic identifiers can be mapped to particular links (TID-to-link mapping) {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. Each link contends for the medium independently, which gives traffic another access opportunity on a less busy link; a device in [[emlsr|EMLSR]] mode exchanges frames on one link at a time {{emlsr-what}}.
beats.sceneDescription: Grey upload traffic fills the 5 GHz link. The voice packets move onto the 6 GHz link and keep arriving at the badge, while the 2.4 GHz link stands ready.

beats.heading: Earlier Wi-Fi: one lane at a time

caption.headline: Earlier Wi-Fi: one lane at a time
caption.takeaway: Before Wi-Fi 7, switching bands meant reconnecting{{single-link-pre-be}}; with MLO the other lanes are already open.
caption.technical: Password-based sign-in over multi-link connections requires [[wpa3|WPA3]]{{wpa3-mlo-required}}.

beats.body:
Before Wi-Fi 7, a device was connected on one band at a time. If that band became busy, it could only wait or move to another band — which meant reconnecting, briefly pausing traffic.

With Wi-Fi 7, the other links are already set up, so traffic can move without reconnecting first {{mlo-tid-mapping}}.
beats.bottomLine: The same building and access points carry voice and urgent data more steadily, because traffic no longer waits for one congested band.
beats.deepDive: Earlier band steering and roaming move a client by disassociating and reassociating on another band or access point, so traffic pauses during the change. MLO keeps all links associated under one security context {{mlo-tid-mapping}}. Password-based authentication over Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections requires [[wpa3|WPA3]] {{wpa3-mlo-required}}.
beats.sceneDescription: The view splits in two. On the left, an earlier-generation connection uses a single link that clogs with upload traffic while voice packets wait. On the right, the Wi-Fi 7 connection has three links open, and the voice packets move to the free one and keep flowing.

questions.q: Does MLO replace roaming between access points?
questions.a: No. MLO links one device to one multi-link access point across its bands{{mlo-defined-be}}. Moving between access points is still roaming, so roaming design still matters.
Password-based sign-in over Wi-Fi 7 multi-link connections requires WPA3{{wpa3-mlo-required}}, so plan the WPA3 migration together with the MLO rollout.

beats.heading: How much a device gains depends on its mode

caption.headline: Gains depend on each device’s mode
caption.takeaway: Some devices use several links at once; others switch between them. Check each model before buying.
caption.technical: [[str|STR]] sends and receives on links at once{{str-what}}; [[emlsr|EMLSR]] listens on several, exchanging data on one{{emlsr-what}}.

beats.body:
Clinicians move constantly, and the traffic that matters most — voice calls, alerts, [[telemetry|telemetry]] — is small but time-sensitive. MLO helps that traffic route around a busy band instead of waiting behind it.

How much it helps depends on both ends. A device in [[str|STR]] mode can use links at the same time {{str-what}}; one in [[emlsr|EMLSR]] mode listens on several links but exchanges data on one at a time {{emlsr-what}}. Current client devices differ, so check the mode, link count and firmware of each badge, phone and laptop model (see **MLO modes** below).
beats.bottomLine: Plan MLO alongside device refresh: the access points enable it, but each clinical device model determines how much benefit it actually receives.
beats.sceneDescription: Four small panels, one per multi-link mode, each with an access point, a device and two links. STR: both links active at once. NSTR: the links take turns. EMLSR: the device listens on both but exchanges data on one at a time. EMLMR: both links active, with the device’s radio streams shifting between them.

questions.q: Will our current badges and phones get MLO?
questions.a: Only if they support Wi-Fi 7 multi-link operation, which needs new hardware. Ask vendors which multi-link mode each model supports, how many links it uses and with which firmware{{mlo-modes-be}}; it decides how much benefit the device sees.

keyFigures.metric: Bands one connection can hold links in
keyFigures.note: How many links carry traffic at the same time depends on the device’s multi-link mode.

keyFigures.metric: Moves traffic between bands without reconnecting

sections.heading: MLO modes: STR, NSTR, EMLSR and EMLMR
sections.body:
IEEE 802.11be defines several ways a device can use multiple links {{mlo-modes-be}}. Each is a behaviour, not a radio count:

**[[str|STR]] (simultaneous transmit and receive)** — the device can send on one link while receiving on another {{str-what}}. It gives the most concurrency but needs good isolation between bands.

**[[nstr|NSTR]] (non-simultaneous)** — the device has multiple links but cannot send on one while receiving on another, so their timing is coordinated.

**[[emlsr|EMLSR]] (enhanced multi-link single radio)** — the device listens on several links but exchanges frames on only one at a time {{emlsr-what}}. It suits devices with one main radio, though the mode does not fix how many radios a device has.

**[[emlmr|EMLMR]] (enhanced multi-link multi-radio)** — the device moves its transmit and receive spatial streams between links as traffic needs {{emlmr-what}}.

These modes are not a simple ladder from cheap to best. Which one a badge, phone, laptop or access point supports is a product decision, so check the mode, link count and firmware during procurement.
